source: User-provided AQA Germany revision guide, first ten photographed pages; content paraphrased and restructured for revision use.

extraFacts: The German Empire was created in 1871 after Prussia united many German-speaking states.
The Kaiser held ultimate authority and appointed the Chancellor and ministers.
The Bundesrat represented the German states, while the Reichstag was elected by adult men over 25.
The Reichstag could debate and vote on laws, but it did not control the government in the way a modern UK parliament does.
retrievalQuestions: When was the German Empire created?
Which German state dominated the creation of Germany?
Who appointed the Chancellor?
What was the difference between the Bundesrat and the Reichstag?
examLinks: Be ready to explain why Germany had some democratic features but was still strongly authoritarian.
A strong answer distinguishes elected representation from real control over the government.

extraFacts: Wilhelm II became Kaiser in 1888, when rapid industrial growth was transforming Germany.
By 1913 Germany was producing more iron and steel than Britain and roughly as much coal.
Industrial growth made many factory owners wealthy, while many workers faced low wages and poor working conditions.
Trade unions and the SPD grew as workers demanded political influence and better conditions.
Some socialists favoured reform through parliament, while communists wanted much more radical change.
retrievalQuestions: Why did industrialisation increase support for socialism?
What did the SPD want to change?
How did moderate socialists differ from communists?
examLinks: Link industrial growth to both Germany's strength and rising social tension.
Do not assume that a large SPD vote meant the SPD controlled the government.

extraFacts: Militarism was deeply influential in Imperial Germany and the Kaiser admired military power.
Weltpolitik aimed to increase German power and overseas influence.
A series of Navy Laws between 1898 and 1912 expanded the German fleet.
Building a larger navy and army required higher taxation and borrowing, adding to government debt.
retrievalQuestions: What was Weltpolitik?
Why did the Kaiser want a larger navy?
How did naval expansion create domestic problems?
examLinks: For consequence questions, connect military expansion to taxation, debt and political tension at home.

extraFacts: By 1918 the war had badly damaged Germany's economy and living standards.
War production reduced the supply of ordinary consumer goods and shortages encouraged a black market.
Food shortages and inflation hit workers hard, while some businesses profited from wartime contracts.
Around two million German soldiers died during the First World War.
Women took on more industrial work during the war, disrupting older social expectations.
Strikes and political unrest increased as war weariness spread.
A naval mutiny at Kiel in late October 1918 helped trigger wider revolt and workers' and soldiers' councils.
Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November 1918 and the armistice was signed on 11 November.
retrievalQuestions: Give one economic, one social and one political impact of the First World War on Germany.
Why did unrest increase in 1918?
What happened at Kiel?
When did Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicate?
examLinks: For an impact question, separate economic, social and political consequences.
Use the Kiel mutiny and abdication to show how wartime problems contributed directly to the collapse of monarchy.

extraFacts: The Weimar Republic introduced a much more democratic constitution after the Kaiser abdicated.
The President was elected for seven years and appointed the Chancellor.
Proportional representation made votes translate fairly into seats but often produced coalition governments.
Article 48 allowed the President to use emergency powers, a weakness that later became increasingly important.
The Treaty of Versailles imposed territorial losses, military restrictions, reparations and the war-guilt clause on Germany.
Reparations were fixed at 132 billion gold marks in 1921.
When Germany fell behind with payments, French and Belgian forces occupied the Ruhr in January 1923.
The government backed passive resistance and printed money to support striking workers, accelerating hyperinflation.
Hyperinflation wiped out many people's savings, while some borrowers found debts became easier to repay.
The Spartacist uprising, Kapp Putsch and Munich Putsch showed that the republic faced threats from both left and right.
retrievalQuestions: What powers did the President have under the Weimar Constitution?
Why could proportional representation be both a strength and a weakness?
What were the main terms of the Treaty of Versailles?
Why did France and Belgium occupy the Ruhr in 1923?
Why did passive resistance contribute to hyperinflation?
Name one left-wing and two right-wing challenges to Weimar democracy.
examLinks: When judging the Weimar Constitution, balance democratic strengths against structural weaknesses such as coalition instability and Article 48.
For hyperinflation, explain the chain: reparations pressure → Ruhr occupation → passive resistance → money printing → rapid loss of currency value.

triggers: treaty of versailles caused hyperinflation by itself
extraMisconceptions.correction: Versailles created financial pressure, but the immediate 1923 hyperinflation crisis was intensified by the Ruhr occupation, passive resistance and the government's decision to print money.

extraFacts: Stresemann ended passive resistance in the Ruhr and helped stabilise the currency with the Rentenmark.
The Dawes Plan of 1924 restructured reparations and brought substantial American loans into Germany.
The Locarno Treaties of 1925 improved relations with western European powers.
Germany joined the League of Nations in 1926.
The Young Plan of 1929 reduced the overall reparations burden and extended repayment.
The mid-1920s saw a cultural revival in art, film, literature and nightlife, especially in major cities.
Recovery remained vulnerable because Germany relied heavily on US loans and political extremism had not disappeared.
retrievalQuestions: How did Stresemann help stabilise Germany after 1923?
What did the Dawes Plan do?
How did Germany's international position improve between 1924 and 1929?
Why was recovery still fragile?
examLinks: Avoid describing the 1920s as a complete recovery: economic and diplomatic gains were real, but important weaknesses remained.

extraFacts: Before the Depression the Nazis were a fringe party: in the 1928 Reichstag election they won only 12 seats.
The Depression caused mass unemployment and bank and business failures, undermining confidence in moderate politicians.
By 1932 German unemployment was around six million.
Fear of communism helped the Nazis appeal to some middle-class voters, farmers and business owners.
Hitler's speaking style, Goebbels' propaganda and the image of an organised, disciplined movement helped attract support.
The Nazis promised jobs, strong leadership, national revival and rejection of Versailles.
The SA gave the party a visible street presence and intimidated opponents.
Nazi support rose sharply after 1929, though it did not rise continuously and the party never won a majority in a free Reichstag election.
retrievalQuestions: How many Reichstag seats did the Nazis win in 1928?
Why did the Depression make extremist parties more attractive?
Give three reasons why Nazi propaganda was effective.
Which social groups could be attracted by fear of communism?
examLinks: For questions on Nazi growth, combine economic crisis with Nazi organisation, Hitler's appeal, propaganda and fear of communism.
Do not treat the Depression as a single automatic cause of Hitler becoming Chancellor.

extraFacts: The Nazis became the largest Reichstag party in July 1932 but still lacked a majority.
Nazi support fell in the November 1932 election, although they remained the largest party.
Political deadlock and repeated changes of Chancellor weakened confidence in parliamentary government.
Franz von Papen believed Hitler could be controlled within a cabinet dominated by conservative politicians.
President Hindenburg finally appointed Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933.
Different groups supported the Nazis for different reasons, including fear of communism, promises of order and jobs, nationalism and hostility to Versailles.
retrievalQuestions: Why did the Nazis still need political deals after becoming the largest party?
What role did Papen play in Hitler's appointment?
Why did Hindenburg eventually agree to appoint Hitler?
Why is it inaccurate to say Hitler was elected Chancellor?
examLinks: Separate Nazi popularity from the political manoeuvring that actually produced Hitler's appointment.
A high-level explanation compares electoral support, Weimar political failure and conservative miscalculation.
